rationale: B wins because it gives the founder the cleaner structural spread. "Going's new AI planner lets the airfare pick the destination" is a real product-behavior story, while A opens with "turns a $200 mistake fare into a booked week" — an invented price wrapped around a booking implication the update does not support. B still sins with "first AI feature," so nobody gets a medal; it just creates fewer messes before the pitch leaves the building.
gaps_in_A: "$200 mistake fare" is invented, and "booked week" implies a completed booking even though the update says no airline or hotel booking happens in-app yet.
"for paying members only" and "A fraction of them get the trip" lean on the same paywall/conversion tension; the consumer and business angles are more overlapping than A admits.
"Two million people get the cheap flight" overstates the supplied fact. The update says Going has about 2 million free members, not that 2 million people receive or book the same cheap flight.

"Next step: newsjack-detector" is the wrong operational instinct unless the founder is actively hunting a fresher peg; the immediate gap is proof: paid-base size, pricing, demo access, booking-roadmap answer, and $550 methodology.
gaps_in_B: "newsletter-born audiences" and "grew a roughly 2-million-member free list as Scott's Cheap Flights" import company history that was not in the update.
"first AI feature" is invented. The facts say Going is launching an AI trip planner, not that this is its first AI product.
"Most trip-planning tools start from a destination" is plausible, but unsourced. Pitch it as a testable framing, not a fact unless Going can prove the contrast.
"category-creation" overstates the first angle. This is a sharp product inversion; it is not a category until usage, competitors, or customer behavior back it up.
